1115691: The school diaries of writer and scholar Ilze Sperga, begun in 1993. Everyday childhood experiences and school events in the 1990s are accompanied by colourful drawings, pasted images and collages created by the author.
1116161: The memoirs of Ruta Lūse (1932–2012), former chair of the Mazsalaca Executive Committee.
1133883: Written in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Augusts Heinrihsons’s (1917–1996) autobiography, ‘My Unusual Life Story’, vividly portrays his childhood and youth in Latvia in the 1920s and 1930s, focusing on everyday life, experiences and joys in independent Latvia. The seemingly cheerful account in the first part of the memoir is disrupted by 1940, when the author becomes a witness to and participant in some of Latvia’s most tragic twentieth-century events. The memoir recounts the deportations of 1941 and the execution of officers, the Nazi German occupation, participation in the Second World War, the brutal Soviet filtration camps, the author’s activities as a Forest Brother, and life in the Latvian SSR in the 1940s and 1950s.
1134078: Two pages from the diary of twelve-year-old Ērika Jurča (1932–1944). They describe Soviet air raids on Riga in September and October 1944.
1135449: Pēteris Treimanis’s (1912–1997) memoir notebook describes his conscription into the Latvian Legion in 1944, combat and life in prisoner-of-war camps.
1135456: The autobiography of Dzintars Lāzers, born in 1932, written between 1999 and 2010 and recounting his life experiences.
1135459: The ‘Work Journals’ of Paulis Alksnis, born in 1904 in Bauņi, Matīši parish. Written from 6 May 1926 to 1931, they document his life and farming at ‘Jaundruķi’ in Augstroze.
1135846: An unknown man’s diary entitled ‘Nature’, written in Russia between 1915 and 1919. It contains brief notes on observations of nature and outdoor activities.
1135955: Astrīda Tobe’s diary, written from 1999 to 2009, recounts her family’s experiences while travelling around Latvia.
1146801: Since July 2018, Uldis Ķirsis has used his Twitter microblog to write about life after moving to the countryside. His concise, witty and perceptive observations describe a city dweller’s rural life in the twenty-first century.
1146882: In memoirs recorded in 1986, Otto Vīksna describes scenes from his childhood near Beja in detail. Structured as several stories, the account offers a broad portrayal of places, villages and their inhabitants, including Beja, Čistigi, Slišiņi and Igauņi. The stories extend well beyond Otto’s own lifetime and surroundings: alongside descriptions of his childhood home, portraits of relatives and vivid accounts of farm life, they outline the wider cultural, historical and economic circumstances of everyday farming life in northern Vidzeme in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
1153249: Elīza, a Riga resident born in 1995, began keeping diaries in 2001, before starting school, and continues to write them. The first diary begins with colourful drawings and gradually develops, as she learns to write, into a record of everyday emotions and events.
1165277: Astra Sleže, then Brīvmane, began her diary in 1971 as a fifteen-year-old girl in Liepāja and continued it during her studies in Jelgava. It records a young woman’s everyday concerns, relationships with peers and philosophical reflections, as well as questions about the purpose of keeping a diary.
1165988: Alvils Kalnietis (Klēbahs, 1876–1958) was a teacher, an advocate for the Latvian language, a journalist and an intellectual in independent Latvia. His diaries from 1926 to 1956 record events and reflections day by day.
1166033: Lizete Strautniece’s diary, written between 1927 and 1933.
1166034: Baiba Zīle’s diaries, written from 1983 to 1992, begin as written records of childhood surrounded by colourful drawings and develop into accounts of events and feelings during adolescence. Everyday life often takes literary form, with the narrative alternating between Baiba’s own creative writing and philosophical reflections.
1169773: Alfrēds Baltbārdis’s (1918–2003) diaries, written between 1948 and 1988.
1166035: Aina Rizga (1936–2015) of Sunākste wrote her life story in 2013. Initially intended as memories of her youth at open-air dances, it developed into a life story organised in chronological chapters.
1174752: The memoirs of gardener Pēteris Lucāns (1900–1992), written from 1979 to 1990. They recount the history of the Lucāns family and the author’s eventful life, his years in exile and everyday life in a labour camp, his return to the Latvian SSR, his working life and his family.
1172883: Jānis Golvers’s autobiographical account, ‘Information about Our Family’, was written in 1956. The memoir relates the legend behind the Golvers family surname and describes an extensive network of relatives. It follows the author through the First World War and the Latvian War of Independence, and records a Vainiži farmer’s everyday observations, the changing seasons, the consequences of collectivisation and the family’s most tragic experiences, when some members were deported to Siberia.
1173264: Gaida began her diaries in 1966, when she was in the seventh grade. Until 1969, she recorded her everyday life, including household and farm chores, school and events in Mazsalaca, alongside poetry she wrote herself.
1174715: The diaries of Paulīne Ārgale, a home economics teacher at Jeri Primary School from 1948 to 1958, describing the everyday routines and challenges of school life.
1172699: Jānis Valters Čoka’s (1927–1989) recollections of the summer of 1940 were written in the 1950s. He describes a summer spent at ‘Kangari’ near Mazsalaca, tending a garden for the Mazpulki youth organisation. The memoir offers a romantic account of his youth, carefree days and first love.
1289462: In 2016 and 2017, Madara compiled the written memories of her grandmother Rasma, born in 1929, in the blog ‘Grandma’s Stories’.
1176873: The collection consists of two parts: Vilma Valentīne Heinrihsone’s (1918–2011) diary entries from 1940, and memoirs written in the 1980s and 1990s about the Second World War and its aftermath.
1179135: Cēzars Aleksis’s (1895–1976) memoirs recount his childhood and schooling, studies at the Pskov surveying school and work as a military topographer. They also describe his involvement in the Troitsk Battalion and life as a forester in newly independent Latvia up to 1925. A separate chapter is devoted to his family and the fates of his relatives.
1179257: Written in 1948, Jānis Auzenbahs’s (1896–1948) memoirs bring together a family chronicle and his own life story: childhood, fighting in the First World War, an injury, life as a teacher and a new smallholder in independent Latvia, and the events of the Second World War.
1179344: The diaries of poet and journalist Lija Blūma (born 1953).
1181543: Arvīds Fēlikss Latsons’s (1897–1945) diaries, written in 1944 and 1945, record his experiences as a refugee and trace his journey from Omuļi parish to the Fischbach refugee camp.
1185814: Aleksandra Eihe’s (1905–2002) life story was written in the 1990s. She looks back on her childhood in Siberia, her youth in Latvia and her adult life, which she spent in exile in Sweden.
1185819: Elīna Vilmane-Meženiece’s blog about volunteering in Samara, Russia, in 2011–2012.
1186759: Mirga Iveta Kuļikovska’s (1927–1997) diary was written from 1941 to 1944. A schoolgirl at the time, she describes life under Nazi occupation, including the war, classmates, studies and growing up.
1186829: Velta Vītola’s (1903–2002) memoirs, written between the 1970s and 1990s, recount her childhood in Moscow, her youth in Latvia, her studies at the Moscow Academy of Arts and her work as a teacher in various Latvian schools. The account symbolically concludes in 1937, when she marries.
1190647: Uldis Pudelis’s (1929–2016) recollections of childhood in Mazsalaca parish in the 1930s and of everyday life and work as an agronomist in the Soviet Union.
1192809: Kārlis Kreicmanis’s (1903–1984) recollections of the ‘Bēkas’ homestead, Ķoņi and the Rūjiena area during the First and Second World Wars.
1187225: Aleksandrs Kudiņš’s (1919–2004) memoirs cover his entire life. They recount his childhood in a Latgalian village in Siberia, his education, everyday life in the USSR in the 1920s and 1930s, the Second World War and his work as a teacher in the Latvian SSR after the war.
1203198: Ziedone Sērmūkša’s memoir miniatures form a literary life story about her childhood in independent Latvia, a young musician’s dreams and hopes, Latvian musical and theatrical circles after the Second World War, and the Soviet literary world and the particular challenges of translation.
1197004: The authors of ‘Voyage Notes’ are three researchers, Kārlis, Sašs and Andis, graduates of the University of Latvia Faculty of Biology who were recruited from different laboratories for a research voyage in the Baltic Sea in December 1959. From the outset, they expected long passages with little research work, while winter conditions would prevent them from enjoying the sea views. They would have to spend long periods in cramped cabins, struggling with seasickness. To make daily life on board more interesting, Sašs suggested keeping a collective diary.
1283651: Žanis Tālbergs’s diary, written in a labour camp in Kolyma, records events from May to November 1946. It documents harsh everyday life, working conditions, meals and daily routines. These stark accounts alternate with romantic dreams of his homeland and returning home.
1207861: Betija Grava’s (1902–1995) diaries were written at different times: the earliest dates from 1917 and the latest from the late 1960s.
1203200: Lilija Auzenbaha’s (1898–1973) memoir recounts her family’s flight from their home in Lestene parish to Riga in 1915, and from Riga to Vidzeme in 1917. The young woman’s notes were written in Valka in 1917 and 1921. They offer detailed accounts of refugees’ everyday lives and feelings during their journeys.
1205071: Vineta Beltiņa’s memoirs were written in the early twenty-first century, looking back on her life. She reflects on her childhood and her parents’ work on the Pārgauja collective farm, her schooling and working life, and her various relationships and experiences of love.
1205720: Part of the material recorded by Kārlis Svensons (1884–1964) throughout his life: quotations, poems, copied passages of literature and translation exercises. This extensive material was compiled by his grandson Andris after Svensons’s death. There are more than one hundred notebooks; in three of them, the author recounts his own life, from his parents’ marriage in Sweden in the late nineteenth century to his final years in Latvia in the 1950s and 1960s.
1211235: The collection contains autobiographical writings by Silvija Priedniece, née Grēniņa, begun in the 1990s: an autobiographical account covering her entire life, alongside diary entries recording everyday events from 1995 onwards.
1206968: Emīlija Vecvagare worked as a secretary in the Provisional Government’s office and kept her diary from 21 July 1917 to 31 December 1921. It is rich in the young woman’s personal feelings and observations of events in Liepāja. Particularly noteworthy are the entries describing the coup in Liepāja on 16 April 1919, during the Latvian War of Independence.
1209459: The diary of woodworking engineer and educator Gunārs Viļums (1945–1989), entitled ‘With a Shotgun and a Fishing Rod’. Written from 1971 to 1977, it records hunting and fishing adventures.
1209573: Diary entries written in Līgatne in 1951 describe the birth and childhood of Egita Balode-Logina’s father. Notes written there in 1975 document Egita’s own arrival in the family, portraying her parents’ feelings as they raise their first child.
1214933: From 16 July to 9 August 1964, a group of tourists from Latvia travelled through six Soviet republics: Russia, Ukraine, Moldova, Belarus, Lithuania and Latvia. They recorded their experiences and observations in a shared diary.
1217832: The diaries and notes of poet Andrejs Pablo Mierkalns, written in 1954 and 1959.
1217237: Artūrs Krūms’s recollections of eleven women in his life, written in 1954 under the title ‘Shadows of the Past’.
1268074: The diary of ceramic artist and long-serving Liepāja Theatre employee Velta Sproģe (1902–1997), written in the 1920s and 1930s and resumed after a break in 1955. It records everyday events and experiences until 1963.
1261070: Photographer Nikolajs Brīvlauks’s (1928–2003) recollections of the end of the Second World War, when, aged just sixteen, he was conscripted into air defence service and became involved in the war.
1276648: The German-language diary of Baltic German Anna Koch, covering the periods 1826–1837 and 1863–1864.
1270711: The diaries of artist Jānis Sudmalis (1887–1984), founder and long-serving director of Liepāja Museum. The first diary was written in 1939–1940; the next available diary dates from 1973 and is followed by regular daily entries until 1981.
1276664: The Vecsētas manor cash book (1900–1902) contains not only records of various expenses, but also unrelated everyday notes written by an unidentified person in Russian and Latvian between 1914 and 1917.
1245358: Architecture student R. Āboliņš’s notes on the excavation of the ruins of the war-damaged House of the Black Heads in 1941.
1246190: Sculptor Jānis Zibens’s professional diary records his work and various events while carving an element of the Freedom Monument in 1935.
1246844: The correspondence between Andis Mitāns (born 1935) and Gunārs Skubiņš (born 1934) covers 1958–1960. The two childhood friends began exchanging letters regularly after graduation, when Andis started working in Riga and Gunārs’s work took him to Jaungulbene.
1247341: Former history teacher and local historian Mečislavs Vertinskis’s (born 1932) recollections of childhood and everyday life around Dagda. Written in Russian in 2011.
1247401: The memoirs of Anna Vagale (born 1918), a former Latvian language and literature teacher and enthusiastic local historian, about her native village of Mateļi. She incorporates folklore materials, including folk songs, beliefs and various customs. Written in the late 1980s, the memoir looks back on the village from Anna’s childhood to the Second World War.
1282797: Jānis was born in 1926 at ‘Lejaskliņģeri’ in Vecate parish, where he lived throughout his life. After his death in 2005, his daughter Gaida Pevko found old papers while cleaning the attic. They turned out to be his diaries from 1945–1947. Everyday concerns and duties on the farm, changing temperatures and observations of nature alternate with uncertainty about his own fate and that of his loved ones in Latvia under Nazi German and Soviet occupation.
1290580: In 1955, while in exile in Siberia, blacksmith Voldemārs Mitenieks (1908–1960) began writing his life story, entitled ‘Lonely Hearts’. He completed the first part, describing his childhood near Dobele in a somewhat romantic and poetic, yet candid manner.
1293854: Latvian Legion soldier Imants Jansons’s diary, accompanied by photographs, recounts the experiences and feelings of a nineteen-year-old during the Second World War. The author called it ‘The Book of My Days’, documenting daily life in turbulent circumstances through poetic language and vocabulary characteristic of his native Kuldīga area.
1291616: Marta Vītuma began writing her recollections in 1997, aged eighty-eight. Her daughter Zaiga later typed them up and gave each story a thematic title. Zaiga recalls that writing gave her mother ‘an opportunity to fill lonely hours and to tell us, her loved ones, about important events in her life that would otherwise remain unknown’.
1295128: Jēkabs Ziedars’s (born 1924) memoir, entitled ‘Puišķins, Anūts, Džeks’. Written in the third person, it recounts his childhood in Silene, Latgale, studies at Liepāja Technical School, involvement in the Second World War and time in the prisoner-of-war camp at Zedelgem. His studies at the Baltic University are particularly important in the account. The final part describes his journey to Australia and his first years there.
1306961: Herta Egle’s (1913–2004) life story focuses on major milestones: childhood in Anna parish, studies at the Ranka Home Economics School, marriage, the upheavals of the Second World War, years in exile in Siberia, and everyday life in the Latvian SSR after returning home.
1307411: The life story of Adolfs Čerbikovs (1921–2013), a resident of Anna parish in the Alūksne region, recorded in 2006 by his granddaughter Līva Čerbikova. It recounts his experiences in the Latvian Legion during the Second World War and in Soviet penal camps, followed by life after returning to his father’s homestead. He remained actively involved in the cultural life of Anna parish until the end of his life.
1311836: Aivars Puzulis of Alūksne recorded his recollections of his native village of Mazuļi between April 2013 and May 2014. His mother had been the village’s last resident. Accounts of villagers, including Aivars’s parents and grandparents, houses and events are accompanied by an extensive collection of place names from Mazuļi and its surroundings.
1307228: Romāns Dūnis’s (1925–2019) memoirs, written in 2003, recount his childhood in Valmiera. They offer a vivid portrayal of the town in the 1930s, describing family members and relatives, his father Jānis Dūnis’s publishing business, its employees and the processes involved in producing books.
1307590: Alberts Baltturs’s (1899–1980) diaries, written from 1975 to 1979. Alongside weather observations and a work journal, they contain his poems, quotations, newspaper clippings and drawings, conveying his inner life. The diary entries are in Russian; the poems are in both Russian and Latvian.
1307973: The collection includes Elizabete Buša’s (1891–1981) memoirs, written in 1916, of her family’s flight from Sloka to Russia, poems written in the early twentieth century, and a separate notebook of poems from the 1970s.
1312689: Juris Emsiņš’s (born 1936) recollections of his childhood and youth in Lielvārde. Particular attention is paid to Lielvārde Secondary School and his studies, the ‘Lāčplēsis’ collective farm’s folk dance group, initially led by Harijs Sūna and later by Uldis Šteins, and sporting events.
1311692: The diary documents scouting activities in 1938–1939. The boys informally describe discussions and activities at scout meetings. Combining criticism with friendly teasing, they record knowledge gained from lectures, skills acquired in practical sessions and shared experiences on several trips. The text is accompanied by drawings, newspaper clippings and photographs.
1312690: Aija Vīksna’s (born 1929) recollections of Vecdzērve, a village in Sauka parish where she was born and spent her early years. The memoir describes all the village’s houses in the 1930s, its most memorable inhabitants and notable events.
1313135: Lūkass Ozoliņš’s (1879–1962) memoirs, written in Buffalo, USA, in 1959. The first part brings together information about his family, including his grandparents Fricis and Made Ozoliņš and his father Jēkabs Ozoliņš. The concluding part recounts his own life: the 1905 Revolution and the flight that followed, the First World War, service as a member of Latvia’s parliament, teaching in various Latvian schools, emigration to displaced persons camps in Germany and his final years in Buffalo.
1336311: Marfa Mivrenika’s (born 1937) recollections of a carefree and happy childhood in Viļāni, disrupted in 1944 when partisans killed her father. The subsequent account chronologically describes life on a collective farm and the realities of the early Soviet period.
1352592: Forester Edgars Ezerlīcītis’s (1927–2015) memoirs, written in the early twenty-first century, look back on his life and examine forest management around Jūrmala. He describes flora and fauna, soil characteristics, lakes and rivers in detail, alongside various hunting experiences. The account contains extensive factual and scientific information, yet the narrative is fluent and at times poetic.
1336271: Emīls Kriškāns (1908–2000), a Latvian living in Lithuania, wrote these memoirs in 1979 about his childhood and his family home, ‘Kalneļi’. He reconstructs his family history in detail and records everyday events and personal experiences.
1328742: Historian Pēteris Stepiņš’s (1914–1999) memoirs, written in 1995, about his native village of Anči in Auleja parish. Written in a distinctive mixture of Latvian and Latgalian, they recount personal memories of everyday village life in the 1920s.
1360382: Genovefa Upeniece’s (born 1945) diaries record everyday events and personal experiences from 1959 to 2018.
1375693: The collection contains the diaries of Zigrīda Paegle (born 1945) of Jūrkalne. The earliest dates from 1961; the more recent diaries were written from 1999 onwards. Initially, they record practical information such as weather, farm figures including milk yields and hatched eggs, debts incurred or repaid, and dates of deaths. Over time, the entries become more personal and detailed. Zigrīda describes what she has done on particular days and reflects on her emotions. Read together, the diaries show how a notebook develops into a deeply felt means of self-therapy.
1378773: A young woman’s thoughts and emotions recorded in diary form in the 1990s.
1379002: Jāzeps Puksts wrote his only diary in 1951 while serving in the Soviet Army in the Ukrainian city of Berdychiv.
1362666: Dāvis Dauvarts, owner of the ‘Vecdaudži’ farm in Brenguļi parish, began his fourth diary on 31 December 1931. The final entry was written shortly before his death on 17 September 1944. Entries were made irregularly and often include quotations from literary sources. His wife Olga Dauvarte, née Lappekins, contributes entries in two places. In describing her grandfather’s diary, Ilze Dauvarte highlights the influence of the Moravian Brethren movement.
1367125: The life story of Vija Poļaka (born 1928), a poet from the Gulbene region, written in 2009. The account consists of short miniature pieces recalling the most vivid and significant moments of her life.
1378689: Marija Liepniece’s weather observations and notes recording deaths among her acquaintances and in the surrounding area. Written in the late 1970s and the 1980s, these notes began a tradition continued by her daughter Zigrīda Paegle in her own records. The collection contains writings by both women, illustrating a family tradition of autobiographical record-keeping.
1388011: Vita Neimane’s calendar notes record personal information, such as family and friends’ celebrations, financial matters, illnesses, planned meetings and events, alongside events in the wider world, including politics and the birthdays of well-known people. The collection contains calendars from 2001 to 2019.
1386157: Sailor Kārlis Lapiņš’s (1920–1937) diary, written in 1936–1937 during his first sea voyage aboard the steamship ‘Rasma’. Brief entries record locations, weather, unfamiliar plants and animals, everyday events on board, meals and other observations. The notebook also contains sailors’ songs.
1393308: Scouts L. Zālītis and B. Strads’s account of a cycling trip undertaken on 21–23 October 1938 along the route Riga–Ķekava–Rembate–Jaunjelgava–Koknese–Pļaviņas–Madona–Gaiziņš Hill–Ērgļi–Riga.
1393069: A rifleman’s diary, begun on 23 December 1914.
1410746: Eduards Tančers’s (1909–1994) letters to his future wife Velta, written in 1936–1937. The collection includes a draft of a poetic love letter and several original letters expressing his longing and affection.
1410773:
The collection contains letters sent by Jānis Tančers to his family in Valmiera. The first group dates from his service in the Soviet Army in 1961–1964; the second consists of letters written while working for the ‘Brīvais vilnis’ fishing collective in Salacgrīva in 1966–1968, when he frequently undertook deep-sea voyages.

The collection also includes Jānis’s recollections and a photograph from the time of the barricades in the 1990s.
1687233: Alma Vucena began writing her memoirs on 22 December 1970, aged seventy-one. They recount her life from birth, including hard work at her parents’ home, the First and Second World Wars, family life and her children, continuing to the end of her life.
1465160: Pēteris Pokrotnieks’s notes on weather observations, events in nature and everyday work completed.
1438382: Political prisoner Līna Zālīte’s prison writings, recorded in Ventspils Women’s Prison in 1935. They include a diary reflecting on daily prison life, life more broadly and politics, alongside songs and poems recorded in prison. Together they shed light on women’s prison culture in independent Latvia during the interwar period.
1448573: A letter sent from Riga by blacksmith’s apprentice Jānis Rudzāns (1888–1919) to his father Juris, discussing the possibility of buying a house near Riga. Written shortly before the First World War, it offers glimpses of the period: difficulties finding work on estates, construction and expansion in Riga, and changes in farming practices.
1451221: Veronika Vītola’s (1940–2020) recollections of the summer of 1954 portray a young girl’s world in the Balvi region, describing both the realities of Soviet life and private family routines, relationships and traditions. The memoir was written in 2001–2002.
1475487: Eustahija Lucjanova’s diary, written from 1 May 1939 to 31 March 1943.
1501853: Geographer Valentīns Pūriņš’s (1910–1998) memoirs, written from 1990 to 1998. In the first part, ‘Scenes from My Life’, he describes his ancestors, the Vilks and Pūriņš families, and an unusual period when he had to spend seven years away from his parents and their home near Saint Petersburg, living in Vecgulbene with his grandparents and his father’s brothers. In the second part, ‘A Life Journey with a Referral from the Siverskaya School Colony’, he recounts his education at various Soviet schools and higher education institutions.
1540385: Pēteris Zariņš’s memoirs, recorded in the 1980s, recount his childhood in Jaunburtnieki after the First World War, farming at his father’s homestead, deportation during the Second World War and life in a labour camp in Inta.
1543863: Skaidrīte Rozīte’s memoirs describe her father Jānis Rozītis, her mother Emma Rozīte and events from her birth to the outbreak of the Second World War.
1589746: Vera Goppers’s memoirs about her husband, General Kārlis Goppers, their first meeting, his military service, participation in the First World War and return to Latvia. The account was written in Sweden in 1949 and 1950. The text was translated from Russian.
1502631: Dzidra Bukaine’s memoirs recount her family history and the wartime and post-war years. She kept a diary throughout her life and compiled her diaries into a life story between 2005 and 2010.
1550804:
The collection contains the diaries and letters of writer, librarian and biographical researcher Austra Rudzīte (1911–1991).

The diaries focus on Jānis Jaunsudrabiņš (1877–1962). Austra began taking notes in 1959, when she attended his wife’s birthday celebration, and subsequently recorded every meeting and conversation with the writer. They vividly document the final years of this classic of Latvian literature, including detailed accounts of his death and funeral.

The second part contains diary entries and notes on documenting Jaunsudrabiņš’s literary and material legacy and establishing a museum devoted to him at the Latvian Gymnasium in Münster.
1529456: From June to November 1977, Jānis Cikota kept ‘A Fisherman’s Notes’ while aboard a Soviet fishing vessel.
1564964: Ernests Slaucītājs’s diary was written from 20 April to 28 May 1945, while he, his family and other Latvians were refugees in Germany.
1636812:
The collection contains Gunars Dambe’s (1925–1979?) letters and travel diaries from the late 1940s and the 1950s. The letters were sent from Esslingen to Koknese, where his parents and younger brother had remained. After living in a displaced persons camp, Gunars emigrated to New Zealand, recording his impressions of the move in letters: nature, people, culture, climate, food and other experiences.
In 1956, Gunars and friends sailed from New Zealand to the USA aboard ‘Taihoa’. His notes also document this voyage.
1636933:
The collection contains the diaries of philosopher Jānis Grīnvalds (1897–1981), later headmaster and history teacher at Riga’s Rainis No. 8 Evening School for Working Youth.

They include wartime diaries from 1940, when Grīnvalds worked in the Red Army’s supply department, and later diaries from 1961 to 1981. These describe his daily life and experiences, documenting the realities of Soviet Latvia over twenty years.
1646639:
In 1950, while expecting the birth of their son, Jānis Grīnvalds and his wife began a diary. After Dainis Grīnvalds was born, Jānis continued to record his son’s life. The diary goes beyond factual notes about first words or steps: Jānis follows his son’s daily experiences and feelings, reflecting on and analysing them in detail.

He also closely follows his son’s schooling, offering an opportunity to examine Soviet education and policy in the late 1950s and the 1960s. Jānis analyses both the curriculum and his child’s adjustment to and place within the school system.

He formally continued these diaries about his son until 1976. Written over a quarter of a century, they provide a vivid record of the period, rich in historical detail.
1636935:
The collection contains entries from Aina Zepa’s (1928–1993) diary, written between 1 May 1944 and 23 May 1946. There is a gap from autumn 1944 to autumn 1945, when Aina was deported to Germany and Austria.

The diary portrays a young woman’s feelings and everyday life in occupied Riga, marked by sentimental reflections, loneliness and longing.
1587294: Pāvils Švābe (1912–2006) recounts the period from his birth to 1992. His memoir describes childhood as a refugee, tending livestock, school, military service, the Second World War and other events in his life.
1593461: F. Celmiņš worked as a bookbinder at Nereta manor. His diary, written from 1913 to 1915, describes everyday work and events: visits, communal work gatherings, open-air dances and flight as a refugee.
1595515: Kārlis Daukste’s memoirs, written in the late 1930s, recall his childhood and youth at the family home, ‘Druķi’, in Krustpils parish. Warmth and humour run through the account.
1595518:
Alfrēds Teodors Žīgurs (1904–1995) began writing his memoirs in the 1980s at the encouragement of the director of the Jēkabpils District Local History Museum. The opening draws on accounts told by his father-in-law Jānis Porietis (1886–1964) and mother-in-law Janīna Poriete, née D’Erseville (1880–1964). Both actively participated in the 1905 Revolution and were forced to emigrate. They lived in Bern at the same time as Lenin and also spent an extended period in London. The narrative traces the lives of revolutionaries and political refugees in Western Europe in considerable detail.
Alfrēds also describes his own family and life. Born in Stradi parish in the Gulbene district, he moved frequently during childhood and lived in Krustpils from 1926 onwards.
Overall, the memoir explores the Žīgurs and Porietis families through both the author’s personal memories and relatives’ accounts.
1636959:
The collection contains the diary of Dailes Theatre actress Ruta Šleiere (1927–2006), written from 1943 to 1947. It vividly records a young woman’s experience of the Second World War. Despite the hardships of the war and post-war years, relationships and feelings dominate the diary. She describes her relationships, troubles in love and existential reflections on her potential vocation and the meaning of human life.
The diary is also filled with cultural references: Ruta reads extensively, records her reflections, frequently attends the theatre and describes her strongest impressions of productions, actors and direction.
1633500:
The memoirs of lawyer and writer Marija Bērziņa, whose real name was Anna Dauge-Šķēris (1906–1986). They describe her father’s Šķēris family and her mother’s Andriņš family, her childhood in Sēlija, flight as a refugee during the First World War, return home and life in independent Latvia. Marija studied law, worked as a lawyer and was actively involved in cultural and literary life.
The memoir also describes the Second World War in detail and a woman’s fate amid historical events that disrupted and fundamentally transformed everyday life.
1636545: In these memoirs, Ligita Vucena describes meeting and working with horticulturist and fruit-tree breeder Pēteris Upītis. The memoirs were written between 1957 and 1989.
1644074: Marta Kapiņa kept her diary from 1925 to 1986. It describes her feelings, troubles in love, dances during her youth, cinema visits and other events she attended. Weather conditions are recorded almost daily. Most entries concern life in Purvciems, Riga, but the diary also recounts living in rural Sēja parish, travelling to Lithuania during the Second World War and visits to other places.
1648999: Luīze Grigāne kept her diary from 1925 to 1978. A teacher trained at the Jelgava Teachers’ Institute, she worked in several places in Latvia, including Valmiera’s six-year primary school. The diary describes her experience as a member of the Latvian Social Democratic Workers’ Party following Kārlis Ulmanis’s coup in 1934, life during the Second World War and post-war work at Mārupe’s six-year primary school. It also recounts the lives of her children and grandchildren.
1652337:
The collection presents the diary entries of Mirdza (1924–2006) and Edgars Laķis (1925–2018) in parallel.

After Mirdza died in 2006, Edgars found her diary while sorting through her belongings. She had begun it in December 1938, aged fourteen, while attending Jaungulbene Home Economics Secondary School. Edgars had also kept a diary for much of his life, beginning in 1943. He decided to transcribe both diaries, following their lives in parallel until they met, and then their shared life and the complications of love. He hoped to publish the manuscript under the pseudonym Edvards Locis but could not find a publisher.

Edgars faithfully transcribed both sets of entries without attempting to alter them or make them more literary. The manuscript also includes occasional reflections, insertions and comments that he wrote in 2006.
1662229:
Alfreds Šķēle began his memoirs on 30 October 1915 while in Tula Governorate, describing the flight as a refugee that he had begun in July that year.

The second notebook is an illness diary, written from 1948 to 1951 after Alfreds contracted tuberculosis.
1689269:
The collection contains letters addressed to actress Malvīne Ustube (1908–1996).

Malvīne was born in Liepāja in 1902, studied acting at the People’s University and moved to Riga in 1929. Under the stage name Malvīne Kaiva, she performed at several theatres, including the Workers’ Theatre, the Small Theatre and the National Theatre. From 1938, she acted at Daugavpils Theatre; after the war, she returned to her native Liepāja.

Over her lifetime, she played hundreds of roles, winning the affection of admirers and audiences. The collection contains letters sent to her from the 1930s onwards throughout her life. They range from acquaintances’ detailed accounts of their lives and impressions of performances to holiday greetings and letters from admirers of her acting.
1689421:
The collection contains ten letters sent by Alīda Ķigule (1902–1936) from Germany and Italy to her father Hermanis Ķiguls and his family in Latvia in the 1920s and 1930s.

Alīda was a Latvian film actress during the interwar period, appearing in various films under the name Aija Valmīra. Her letters reveal an actress’s everyday life and experiences in Western Europe. Despite a successful career, including appearances in well-known films such as the French ‘Judex’ (1934) and modelling work, with an award as the most beautiful blonde in Paris in 1933, she faced financial and emotional difficulties, which she shared with her loved ones.

The collection also contains two items sent to Hermanis Ķiguls by Alīda’s cousin Marta Štrāla, née Ķigule. One announces an engagement in 1936; the other is a letter written in 1946, expressing anxiety and uncertainty about the future.
1690857: Valdis Šķēle’s memoirs and reflections on his own and his family’s lives, begun in 1980.
1799971: Excerpts on musical life from the diaries of Kārlis Paucītis, a Latvian National Opera musician, clarinettist, conductor and editor of several music journals.
1812166:
The collection contains autobiographical material written in Ludza in 1989 by Broņislava Bērziņa, née Ādmine (1903–1993), for her daughter Anna Apša, née Bērziņa (1940–2020). It recounts the history of the Ādmine family and that of her husband’s Bērziņš family from Pāliņi, called Puoleni in Latgalian and Poleņi in the text.

The collection also includes the old wedding song ‘Bitter, Bitter, Bitter!’, transcribed in 2018 by Laima Dimanta from a melody sung by Anna Apša. The song is said to be characteristic of the Rūbāni and Bērzpils areas.
1822798: Diary author Arnolds Zērvens (1914–1985) was born at ‘Dīķi’ in Sīpele. He worked as a blacksmith, remained unmarried and was a chess champion in the Dobele district in the mid-1950s. His diary begins in 1949 and ends that same year when he is called up for military service.
1910061: In late 2023, Pēteris Veģis entrusted the Autobiography Collection with memoirs and photographs belonging to his grandmother, Latvian language teacher Olga Veģe. Born in 1904 in Vecmuiža, Vecpiebalga, in the Cēsis district, Olga wrote her memoirs in Sigulda in 1973. Written in rich Latvian, the account offers a vivid picture of life around Vecpiebalga in the early twentieth century and in Cēsis in later decades. It includes references to the works of Rainis, whose literary legacy Olga played a particular role in documenting.
1910641: Milda Lauberte’s diary was written from 25 March to 15 April 1949 during her deportation journey to Siberia, on pages from a drawing notebook. It is accompanied by poems, song lyrics and short accounts of life in Siberia.
1992090: The collection brings together memoirs and stories submitted to the 2024 competition ‘My First Steps in the Latvian National Awakening’.
